accepted.name: description_word_count
accepted.description: Total length of the event description in words: the c_1..c_100 columns are counts of the 100 most frequent corpus words and c_other is every remaining word, so their sum reconstructs the word count of the original text, which the database never stored. Expect a heavy right tail (mean around 70, median around 45, a small number of very long listings).
accepted.why_it_matters: How much text an organiser wrote is a direct proxy for how serious and well-organised the event is. A one-line stub and a fully written listing draw very different crowds, and the users who keep coming back are the ones engaging with real, well-described events. The brute-force generator only forms pairwise differences and ratios, so a 101-term sum over a bag-of-words block is invisible to it.

accepted.name: rare_word_share
accepted.description: Fraction of the event description made of words OUTSIDE the 100 most common corpus words: lexical specificity. Near 0 means the listing is built almost entirely from generic event boilerplate; near 1 means it carries its own vocabulary (band names, venues, topics). The +1 in the denominator only guards descriptions with zero words. Expect a mean around 0.6.
accepted.why_it_matters: Normalises the vocabulary mix out of the raw length, separating 'long because it is a detailed real event' from 'long because it repeats stock phrases'. Generic boilerplate is the signature of bulk-posted or promotional events, which draw one-off attendance rather than the repeat attendance this task predicts.

accepted.name: boilerplate_word_share
accepted.description: Share of the description taken up by only the ten single most frequent words in the whole corpus (c_1..c_10, ordered by global frequency: their means fall monotonically from 2.33 to 0.62). This is the density of the stock event-listing vocabulary, the head of the Zipf curve, as opposed to rare_word_share which measures its tail. Expect a mean around 0.15-0.20.
accepted.why_it_matters: Head share and tail share are not redundant: an event can be low on both (a mid-vocabulary description) and the pair pins down where on the frequency curve a listing sits. Knowing that the c_ columns are frequency-ORDERED is what makes 'the first ten' a meaningful group rather than an arbitrary subset — a generator that treats them as 101 interchangeable numeric columns cannot construct this.

accepted.name: in_contiguous_us_box
accepted.description: Flag: the event's coordinates fall inside the bounding box of the contiguous United States. 1 for a US-mainland event, 0 otherwise. Note that lat/lng are 42.4 percent null, and a comparison against a missing coordinate is false, so 0 means 'not known to be in the US mainland' rather than 'known to be elsewhere'. Given the country column (United States is 1.07M of the 1.60M geolocated events) expect roughly 0.35-0.45 of all rows to be 1.
accepted.why_it_matters: This is exactly the case where knowing what the columns ARE decides the quantity: a raw lat and a raw lng are two unrelated numbers, and every difference or ratio of them is meaningless, but a conjunction of four thresholds is a place. The user base has two centres of gravity (US and Indonesia/South-East Asia, per the locale mix) with very different event ecosystems and very different repeat-attendance behaviour, and this cleanly splits the event side of that divide without relying on the 49 percent-null free-text city.

accepted.name: dist_from_hub_deg
accepted.description: Angular distance of the event from the platform's geographic centre of mass (the median event location, 39.641N 79.464W), with the longitude term scaled by cos(39.6 degrees) = 0.771 so that a degree of longitude counts the same ground distance as a degree of latitude at that latitude. Roughly 111 km per unit near the hub. Null wherever lat/lng are null. Expect a mode near 0-15 (the US north-east and midwest), a second mass around 25-40 (California, Europe) and a long tail to Asia and Oceania.
accepted.why_it_matters: Turns two raw coordinates into one continuous 'how peripheral is this event' scalar, which the box flag above only answers yes/no. Events far from the dense core sit in thin local markets where a user has few alternatives, so their repeat-attendance dynamics differ systematically from the core. The cos-latitude correction is the part a blind generator cannot invent — without it the quantity is not a distance at all.

accepted.name: responded_to_impression
accepted.description: Whether the user gave ANY explicit verdict on an event that was shown to them, positive or negative, as opposed to silently ignoring it. The two flags encode three states (interested 26.8 percent, not_interested 3.3 percent, no response about 70 percent), so this collapses the two engaged states into one and should be 0 or 1 with a mean near 0.30; a 2 would mean a row marked both ways, which I do not expect to occur.
accepted.why_it_matters: Responsiveness and preference are different things, and the raw flags confound them: 'interested = 0' lumps an explicit rejection together with a user who never looked. Separating 'did they engage at all' from 'what did they say' is the distinction that matters for a repeat-attendance task, where the question is whether the user is an active participant. The brute-force generator forms differences and ratios, not sums, so it produces the polarity (interested - not_interested) but never this.

accepted.name: organic_interest
accepted.description: The user marked interest in an event they were NOT invited to — interest found by browsing or recommendation rather than prompted by an invitation. Only 4.25 percent of impressions are invitations, so this should recover most of the 26.8 percent interested rate; expect a mean near 0.25.
accepted.why_it_matters: Self-driven discovery and invitation-driven attendance are different behaviours with different persistence. A user who seeks out events unprompted has a standing habit and will do it again next week; a user who only ever responds to invitations attends when their friends organise something and not otherwise. That is precisely the distinction user-repeat turns on, and it needs the interaction of the treatment flag with the outcome flag — neither a difference nor a ratio of the two recovers it.

accepted.name: invitation_ignored
accepted.description: The user was genuinely invited to this event and then never answered either way — not a decline, a non-response. Invitations are 4.25 percent of impressions and about 70 percent of impressions get no response, so expect a mean around 0.02-0.04. The value can only be negative if a row were flagged both interested and not_interested, which I do not expect to occur.
accepted.why_it_matters: Ignoring a real invitation is the single most informative negative signal about a user on this platform, and it is strictly stronger evidence than ignoring an algorithmic recommendation, which almost everyone does. Only the three-way interaction isolates it: 'invited' alone is 96 percent uninformative context, and no pairwise combination of the three flags separates 'declined' from 'never replied'.

accepted.name: implausible_birthyear
accepted.description: Flag for a self-reported birth year outside the plausible band for this platform: the column has a hard floor at 1900 and a hard ceiling at 1999, both of which look like a data-entry sentinel and a collection cutoff rather than real births, and the real population sits in a tight 1987-1994 interquartile band. Values below 1970 (age over 42) or above 1996 (age under 16 in 2012) are mostly sentinels, joke entries and misreports. The two conditions are mutually exclusive so the result is 0 or 1; the mean is pulled down 2.3 years below the median by the low tail, so I expect somewhere in the 5-20 percent range to be flagged. Null birthyear (3.9 percent) yields a false comparison and reads as 0.
accepted.why_it_matters: This is the canonical case of an integer column that is a measurement in the middle and a label at the edges — a year of birth in the bulk and a sentinel at 1900. Arithmetic on the raw column silently averages the two together, which is what a blind generator does; the flag says 'this profile field was not filled in honestly'. A user who did not bother to enter a real age is a low-investment account, and low-investment accounts do not come back.
